_: THE case table. ADR-035 §2.10: 'one data file, read by both the pgTAP suite and
Vitest, asserting equality to the centavo. Not two copies of the same expectations.'
The expectations here were NOT derived from this package. They were worked out by
hand in supabase/pgtap/07_money_and_units.sql (plan task 3.5) BEFORE any TypeScript
existed, and lifted across by `id` — that ordering is deliberate and is recorded in
docs/PLAN.md step 3: writing this file first would let it be shaped to whatever an
implementation already does, which is the drift it exists to prevent.
⚠️ EVERY NUMBER IN THIS FILE IS A DECIMAL STRING, NOT A JSON NUMBER. A JSON number
is an IEEE754 double in JavaScript, and 0.073 is not 0.073 in one. §2.5 rule 1 says
no floating point anywhere in the money path; a bare `0.073` here would put one in
the money path at the moment the file is parsed, before any code runs. Both readers
take these as text and scale them to integers themselves.
⚠️ THE HALF-CENTAVO BOUNDARIES ALL SIT IN `round(unit_price × qty)`, NEVER IN THE
TAX STEP. §2.5 asked for 'a half-centavo boundary per tax rate', which reads as
though the tax division has one. It does not and cannot — proved by exhaustion in
07 F9 and F18, and §2.5 now carries the correction. A boundary case placed in the
tax split discriminates nothing and looks correct.

scales._: Decimal places each field carries, matching the applied schema: numeric(12,2) money, numeric(14,6) per-base price, numeric(14,3) base quantity, numeric(5,4) rate.

_: The only two cases that can tell §2.5 rule 6 (half-up AWAY FROM ZERO) from
JavaScript's Math.round (half-up toward +∞). The two agree on every positive
number, so the sign is the only place they differ, and the tax steps cannot
produce a tie — so a discriminating case must be a NEGATIVE line whose
unit_price × qty lands on a half centavo. M8 is the sell side, B6 the buy side.
07 falsifications S6, S14, S23 and S24 are the evidence. Delete either id and
the Vitest guard turns red rather than the suite quietly losing its teeth.
